chapters.title: Pattern & strategy: ARD + ESI decide your rank

cards.title: Qualifying vs merit sections
cards.body: In Phase I, Reasoning, English, Computer, Quant and Decision Making are **qualifying**. **GA (20) + ESI (40) + ARD (40) = 100 marks** decide who goes to Phase II. So ARD and ESI are worth 80% of the merit portion.

cards.title: One preparation for both phases
cards.body: Phase II Paper II tests the **same ESI and ARD** with descriptive answers. Make notes in an answer-ready format (definition, data, issues, way forward) from the start so Phase I and II prep overlap fully.

cards.body: 10 marks of situational questions on ethics and organisational judgment. Choose answers that are **lawful, fair, consultative and farmer-centric**, avoiding both inaction and rule-breaking.

cards.title: Data sources
cards.body: Use the Economic Survey (agriculture and social chapters), Union Budget, NABARD's annual report, PIB releases on the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, and the latest Agriculture Census data.

cards.explain: GA + ESI + ARD (100 marks) decide shortlisting; the rest are qualifying.

cards.q: How many marks does the NABARD Grade A interview carry?

notes.h: Phase I: qualifying and merit sections
notes.p:
NABARD Grade A (Assistant Manager, RDBS) has **Phase I**, **Phase II** and an **Interview**. In Phase I, **Reasoning (20), English (30), Computer (20), Quant (20) and Decision Making (10)** are **qualifying**, while **General Awareness (20), ESI (40) and ARD (40)** — **100 marks** — form the merit used to shortlist for Phase II. Check the latest notification for exact numbers and timings.

So **ESI and ARD together carry 80% of Phase I's merit portion**. Your preparation priority should reflect this.
points: Qualifying sections: clear cut-offs, no need to over-invest.
Merit sections: GA + ESI + ARD = 100 marks.
Phase II and the interview (50 marks) decide final selection.

notes.h: Worked example: where marks come from
notes.p:
Merit portion = 100 marks.
ARD share = 40 ÷ 100 = **40%**; ESI = **40%**; GA = **20%**.
Suppose you can improve by 8 marks either in ARD (with focused scheme and agronomy revision) or in GA (current affairs). Each mark has equal value, but ARD's syllabus is more **predictable** (static agriculture plus schemes), so marks there are usually cheaper to earn than in GA's unlimited current affairs.
Meanwhile, qualifying sections only need to cross the cut-off: an extra 5 marks in Quant above the cut-off adds **nothing** to your merit.
Phase II tests the **same ESI and ARD** with descriptive answers (and an English paper). Make notes in an **answer-ready format** from the start so Phase I and Phase II preparation overlap fully.
points: **Definition:** one or two lines.
**Data:** latest Economic Survey, Budget, Agriculture Census or NABARD figures.
**Issues:** 3–4 short points.
**Government measures:** named schemes with launch year.
**Way forward:** 3–4 practical points tied to rural India.

notes.p:
Decision Making has **10 marks** of situational questions on ethics and organisational judgment. Choose answers that are **lawful, fair, consultative and farmer-centric**. Avoid both extremes: doing nothing, and breaking rules to achieve a good outcome.

**Example:** A local leader pressures you to sanction a loan to an ineligible borrower. Best response: politely refuse, explain the eligibility rules, suggest eligible alternatives (such as an SHG route), and inform your superior. This is lawful, transparent and still helpful.
Rely on official, current sources.

notes.h: Crops, intensity and inputs: worked examples
notes.p:
Kharif (monsoon): rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut. Rabi (winter): wheat, mustard, gram, barley. Zaid (summer): watermelon, cucumber, moong.

**Cropping intensity** = gross cropped area ÷ net sown area × 100.
**Worked example 1:** net sown area = 100 ha; 50 ha of it is cropped twice.
Gross cropped area = 100 + 50 = 150 ha. Cropping intensity = 150 ÷ 100 × 100 = **150%**.

**Fertiliser:** urea is **46% nitrogen**.
**Worked example 2:** to supply 92 kg N per hectare, urea needed = 92 ÷ 0.46 = **200 kg**.
Check: 200 × 0.46 = 92 ✓.

chapters.title: ESI (rural focus) & NABARD as an institution

cards.title: NABARD in brief
cards.body: Established **12 July 1982** under the NABARD Act, 1981, on the recommendation of the **CRAFICARD (B. Sivaraman) committee**. Wholly owned by the **Government of India**. Roles: refinance, development (watershed, tribal development, FPOs), and **supervision** of RRBs and cooperative banks.

cards.title: Poverty & inequality
cards.body: Earlier poverty lines: **Tendulkar** (2009) and **Rangarajan** (2014) committees. NITI Aayog's **Multidimensional Poverty Index** uses health, education and living standards (12 indicators in India's version). Inequality is measured with the **Gini coefficient**.

cards.title: Demography & social issues
cards.body: **Demographic dividend**: growth potential when the working-age share is high. Key ESI themes: rural–urban migration, women's labour-force participation, social security for informal workers, nutrition, and education quality.

cards.title: Writing ESI answers
cards.body: Open with a definition and one data point, then cover causes/issues, government measures (named schemes), and a way forward with 3–4 points. Keep each descriptive answer tied to rural India, since that is NABARD's mandate.

cards.q: NABARD was set up on the recommendation of:
cards.explain: The CRAFICARD committee, chaired by B. Sivaraman, recommended NABARD.

cards.q: Which institution supervises RRBs and cooperative banks on behalf of RBI?
cards.explain: NABARD carries out supervision of RRBs and state/district cooperative banks.

notes.p: **NABARD** was established on **12 July 1982** under the **NABARD Act, 1981**, on the recommendation of the **CRAFICARD committee** chaired by **B. Sivaraman**. It took over the agricultural credit functions of the RBI and the refinance functions of the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation. It is now **wholly owned by the Government of India**; its head office is in **Mumbai**.
points: **Financial role:** refinance to banks, RIDF loans to states, long-term irrigation and other funds.
**Developmental role:** watershed and tribal development, FPOs, SHG–bank linkage, rural innovation.
**Supervisory role:** RRBs and state/district central cooperative banks.
**Subsidiaries include:** NABARD Consultancy Services (NABCONS), NABFINS, NABKISAN, NABSAMRUDDHI and NABVENTURES.

notes.p:
Poverty lines in India were based on expert committees: **Tendulkar (2009)** and later **Rangarajan (2014)**. Policy discussion now also relies heavily on the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**. NITI Aayog's national MPI uses **health, education and standard of living**, with **12 indicators** in India's version.

**Worked example: Gini and Lorenz curve.** The Gini coefficient = area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve ÷ total area under the line of equality. If that area ratio is 0.35, Gini = **0.35**. A move from 0.35 to 0.30 means **income is more equally distributed**. Remember: **0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality**.
Key ESI themes with a rural focus.
points: **Demographic dividend:** growth potential when the working-age share of the population is high; needs skills and jobs to be realised.
**Rural–urban migration:** push factors (low farm income) and pull factors (urban jobs).
**Women's labour-force participation:** rising in recent PLFS rounds, driven largely by rural women.
**Social security for informal workers:** e-Shram portal; the four labour codes (brought into force in November 2025; check the current status of their rules).
**Nutrition and education quality:** POSHAN Abhiyaan, the National Education Policy 2020.

notes.p:
**Dependency ratio** = (population aged 0–14 + population aged 65 and above) ÷ population aged 15–64 × 100.

Suppose a district has 300,000 children (0–14), 100,000 elderly (65+) and 800,000 working-age people (15–64).
Dependency ratio = (300,000 + 100,000) ÷ 800,000 × 100 = 400,000 ÷ 800,000 × 100 = **50**.
This means 50 dependants for every 100 working-age people. A falling ratio opens the window for a demographic dividend.

Open with a **definition and one data point**, then cover **causes/issues**, **government measures** (named schemes) and a **way forward** of 3–4 points. Keep every answer tied to **rural India**, since that is NABARD's mandate. For example, an answer on unemployment should discuss rural non-farm jobs, MGNREGA or its successor, DAY-NRLM, skilling and FPO-led value chains.
Key points.

Wholly owned by the Government of India; HQ Mumbai.
Roles: financial, developmental, supervisory.
Poverty lines: Tendulkar (2009), Rangarajan (2014); MPI uses 12 indicators.
Gini 0 = equality; 1 = inequality.

chapters.title: Phase II Paper I: descriptive English (essay, précis, letter, report)

cards.title: What Paper I tests
cards.body: A typed, descriptive paper of 100 marks in 90 minutes, usually with an **essay**, a **précis** or **comprehension**, and a **letter or report**. Topics lean towards rural development, agriculture, banking and the economy.

cards.title: Time plan (90 min)
points: Essay: about 35 minutes
Précis/comprehension: about 25 minutes
Letter/report: about 20 minutes
Revision: 5–10 minutes for typos and word limits

cards.title: Essay structure
points: Introduction: context + a clear thesis (60–80 words)
Body: 3–4 paragraphs, one idea each, with an example or data point
Counter-view or challenges
Conclusion: way forward, linked to the thesis

cards.title: Précis rules
cards.body: Reduce to about **one-third** of the passage, in your own words, third person and past/present tense as appropriate. Keep the central idea and main supports; drop examples, repetition and figures of speech. Add a title if asked.

cards.title: Letters and reports
cards.body: **Formal letter**: sender’s address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body (purpose → details → request), closing. **Report**: title, to/from, date, introduction, findings, recommendations — factual and concise.

cards.q: A précis should usually be about what fraction of the original passage?
cards.explain: Unless the question gives a word limit.

cards.q: Which element should a formal letter NOT contain?
cards.explain: Formal tone throughout.

notes.p: Phase II carries the merit along with the interview, and Paper I is worth 100 of the Phase II marks. Content and clarity matter more than ornate language. Typing speed is part of the test: practise typing answers under time, because handwriting habits do not transfer.

Choose the topic you can support with concrete points. Plan for 3–4 minutes before typing.

**Worked example (outline):** "Role of FPOs in doubling farmers’ income."
Intro: small holdings limit bargaining power; FPOs aggregate.
Body 1: input cost savings through bulk buying.
Body 2: better prices via collective marketing, e-NAM, direct sales.
Body 3: access to credit and technology (NABARD, SFAC support; 10,000 FPO scheme).
Challenges: governance, working capital, professional management.
Conclusion: hand-holding, credit guarantees and market links can make FPOs viable engines of rural income.

**Method:** read twice; underline the main idea of each paragraph; write a rough list of 5–7 points; draft in your own words; count words.

**Worked example:** a 300-word passage → target about **100 words**. If the passage argues that micro-irrigation saves water, raises yields and needs subsidy support, the précis must contain all three ideas in one connected paragraph, without the passage’s examples of particular districts.

In comprehension answers, answer exactly what is asked in complete sentences, using the passage’s information rather than outside knowledge.

**Formal letter (worked structure):** "To the District Collector … Subject: Request for a camp to issue Kisan Credit Cards in X block." Paragraph 1: purpose. Paragraph 2: facts (number of farmers without KCCs, distance to branch). Paragraph 3: specific request and proposed dates. Close with "Yours faithfully", name and designation.

**Report:** use headings — Background, Observations, Recommendations. Keep sentences short and factual; numbers, if any, must be consistent throughout.
points: Use the word limit given; exceeding it can cost marks.
Avoid bullet-only answers unless asked; examiners expect paragraphs.

notes.p:
Good essays need material: two or three facts, a scheme or two, and a balanced view. Keep a running file of themes likely in NABARD papers — climate-resilient agriculture, rural credit, women’s SHGs, digital agriculture, natural farming, rural employment, water conservation, cooperatives — and for each note the problem, government response, NABARD’s role and gaps.

When unsure of a statistic, write qualitatively ("a large share of farmers are small and marginal") rather than inventing numbers. Accuracy and structure earn more marks than impressive-sounding but unverified data.
Avoid these.
points: Writing an essay without a clear thesis.
Copying sentences from the passage into a précis.
Informal tone or abbreviations in letters.
Leaving no time to proof-read typed answers.

notes.p: Paper I checklist.
points: Essay: intro–body–challenges–conclusion.
Précis ≈ one-third, own words, no examples.
Letter: address, date, subject, salutation, body, closing.
Report: background, observations, recommendations.
Practise typing under time.
Read rural and banking editorials for content.

points: Alluvial — Indo-Gangetic plains, deltas; rich in potash, poor in N and P; most extensive
Black (regur) — Deccan plateau; moisture-retentive; ideal for cotton
Red and yellow — iron oxide; Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Chhattisgarh
Laterite — high rainfall, leached; tea, coffee, cashew
Arid, saline/alkaline, peaty, forest/mountain soils

cards.title: Crop seasons
points: Kharif (sown June–July, harvested Sept–Oct): rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, soybean, groundnut, tur
Rabi (sown Oct–Dec, harvested Mar–Apr): wheat, barley, gram, mustard, lentil
Zaid (Mar–June): watermelon, cucumber, moong, fodder

cards.title: Cropping intensity
points: Cropping intensity = gross cropped area ÷ net sown area × 100
Gross cropped area counts land once for each crop grown in a year
Higher intensity → more output from the same land

cards.title: Cropping systems
cards.body: **Monocropping** — one crop repeatedly. **Mixed cropping** — seeds mixed and sown together. **Intercropping** — rows of two crops in a set pattern. **Relay cropping** — next crop sown before harvest of the first. **Crop rotation** — alternating crops (legumes restore nitrogen).

cards.title: Soil reclamation
cards.body: **Acidic** soils are treated with **lime**; **alkaline/sodic** soils with **gypsum**; waterlogged soils need drainage. Soil Health Cards report pH and nutrient status.

cards.q: Which soil is best known for cotton cultivation?
cards.explain: Black (regur) soil retains moisture.

cards.q: Alkaline (sodic) soils are commonly reclaimed using:
cards.explain: Gypsum replaces sodium with calcium.

cards.q: Net sown area 100 ha; gross cropped area 160 ha. Cropping intensity:

notes.p: ARD carries the heaviest weight in NABARD Phase I and is half of Phase II Paper II. Questions on soils, seasons and cropping systems are frequent and factual; descriptive questions link them to productivity, sustainability and farmer income.

ICAR recognises eight major soil groups.

**Alluvial soils** cover the largest area — the Indo-Gangetic plains and coastal deltas. They are fertile, rich in potash but poor in nitrogen and phosphorus.
**Black soils** (regur) of the Deccan form from basalt; they are clayey, swell when wet, crack when dry and retain moisture — ideal for cotton, soybean and pulses.
**Red and yellow soils** owe their colour to iron oxide; they need fertilisers and irrigation.
**Laterite soils** form under heavy rainfall and leaching; suited to plantation crops after manuring.
**Arid soils** (Rajasthan) are sandy and saline; **saline/alkaline** soils need gypsum and drainage; **peaty** soils are rich in organic matter (Kerala, Sundarbans); **forest/mountain** soils vary with altitude.

**Soil health indicators:** pH (6.5–7.5 is near-neutral and suits most crops), organic carbon (often below 0.5% in Indian soils, a sign of low fertility), and available N, P, K plus micronutrients. **Soil erosion** by water and wind removes fertile topsoil; conservation measures include contour ploughing, strip cropping, terracing, mulching and shelterbelts.

India has three seasons: **kharif** (monsoon), **rabi** (winter) and **zaid** (summer). Crops are classified by use: **cereals** (rice, wheat, maize), **millets** (jowar, bajra, ragi — "Shree Anna"), **pulses** (gram, tur, moong, urad, lentil), **oilseeds** (groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower), **fibres** (cotton, jute), **cash/plantation** crops (sugarcane, tea, coffee, rubber).

Rice is mainly kharif; wheat is rabi; maize and some pulses are grown in more than one season.

**Agro-climatic zones:** the Planning Commission identified **15 agro-climatic regions**; ICAR’s NARP divides the country into 127 agro-climatic zones for research planning. Zonal planning helps match crops to rainfall, soil and temperature.

**Worked example 1:** A village has net sown area of 500 ha. In kharif all 500 ha are sown; in rabi 300 ha; in zaid 50 ha.
Gross cropped area = 850 ha.
Cropping intensity = 850 ÷ 500 × 100 = **170%**.

**Worked example 2:** If irrigation lets the farmer sow 200 more ha in rabi, gross cropped area becomes 1,050 ha and intensity rises to **210%** — irrigation is the key driver of cropping intensity.

Crop rotation with legumes (gram, moong) fixes atmospheric nitrogen through **Rhizobium** bacteria, cutting fertiliser needs. Intercropping (e.g. sorghum + pigeonpea) spreads risk and uses resources better.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Lime for acidic soils; gypsum for alkaline soils.
Mixed cropping (no fixed pattern) vs intercropping (rows).
Gross cropped area counts multiple crops on the same land.
Cotton is kharif; mustard is rabi.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Alluvial: most extensive; black: cotton.
Laterite: leached, plantation crops.
Kharif: rice, cotton; rabi: wheat, mustard; zaid: watermelon, moong.
Cropping intensity = GCA ÷ NSA × 100.
Legumes fix nitrogen (Rhizobium).

cards.title: Sources of irrigation
points: Wells and tube wells — largest share of net irrigated area
Canals — major and medium projects
Tanks — traditional in south India
Other sources — lift irrigation, check dams

cards.title: Methods and efficiency
points: Surface (flood, basin, furrow): lowest efficiency
Sprinkler: roughly 70–80% application efficiency
Drip: up to about 90%; saves water and fertiliser (fertigation)
Irrigation intensity = gross irrigated area ÷ net irrigated area × 100

cards.title: PMKSY (2015)
cards.body: **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana**: "Har Khet Ko Pani" and "**Per Drop More Crop**" (micro-irrigation), Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) and watershed development. A **Micro Irrigation Fund** was created with NABARD.

cards.title: Watershed management
cards.body: A **watershed** is the area draining to a common point. Treatment follows a **ridge-to-valley** approach: contour bunds, trenches, check dams, afforestation, and farm ponds, with community participation.

cards.title: Groundwater
cards.body: Over-extraction in states such as Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan has led to falling water tables. **Atal Bhujal Yojana** (2019) promotes community-led groundwater management in selected water-stressed states.

cards.q: The water-application efficiency of drip irrigation can reach about:
cards.explain: Water goes directly to the root zone.

cards.q: "Per Drop More Crop" is a component of:
cards.explain: Micro-irrigation component of PMKSY.

cards.q: Watershed treatment usually proceeds:
cards.explain: Treat upper slopes first to control runoff.

notes.p:
About half of India’s net sown area is irrigated; the rest depends on the monsoon. Irrigation raises yields, allows a second crop and reduces risk. But groundwater depletion, low efficiency of flood irrigation, and water-intensive crops (rice, sugarcane) in dry regions create sustainability concerns — a common descriptive theme.

Rice and sugarcane together consume a large share of irrigation water. Shifting part of the area in water-stressed states to millets, pulses and oilseeds — through procurement support and price incentives — is a common policy suggestion in answers, along with metering of power for pumps and pricing reforms.

**Groundwater** (wells and tube wells) is the largest source of irrigation. **Canals** dominate in parts of the north and in command areas of big dams. **Tanks** are traditional in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Telangana.

**Worked example 1:** A farmer uses 10,000 m³ of water per hectare with flood irrigation at 40% efficiency (4,000 m³ reaches the crop). With drip at 90% efficiency, the same 4,000 m³ requires 4,000 ÷ 0.9 ≈ **4,444 m³** — saving about **55%** of water.

**Worked example 2:** Net irrigated area 80 ha; gross irrigated area 120 ha. Irrigation intensity = 120 ÷ 80 × 100 = **150%**.

**PMKSY (2015)** integrates source creation, distribution and efficient use: AIBP (completing major projects), Har Khet Ko Pani (command-area development, minor irrigation, repair of water bodies), Per Drop More Crop (drip and sprinkler subsidies), and the watershed component. The **Long Term Irrigation Fund** (2016–17) and the **Micro Irrigation Fund** (2018) were set up with NABARD. **Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain** promotes rainwater harvesting, and **Atal Bhujal Yojana** promotes demand-side groundwater management.

Watershed projects treat land and water together: soil conservation on slopes, water harvesting in drainage lines, and livelihood support for landless families. Success depends on community institutions (watershed committees, user groups) and maintenance after project withdrawal. NABARD has supported participatory watershed programmes for decades through its Watershed Development Fund.

**Worked example 3:** A farm pond of 20 m × 20 m × 3 m stores 1,200 m³ (12 lakh litres) of runoff. That is enough for one protective irrigation of about 2 hectares at 60 mm depth (each hectare at 60 mm needs 600 m³) — a cheap insurance against a mid-season dry spell.
points: Key structures: contour bunds, graded bunds, gully plugs, check dams, percolation tanks, farm ponds.
Benefits: higher groundwater, reduced erosion, more cropping intensity.

notes.p: Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Groundwater, not canals, is the largest irrigation source.
Irrigation intensity uses irrigated areas, not cropped areas.
Per Drop More Crop is part of PMKSY.
Ridge-to-valley, not valley-to-ridge.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Drip ≈ 90% efficient; sprinkler 70–80%; flood lowest.
PMKSY 2015: four components.
LTIF and Micro Irrigation Fund with NABARD.
Atal Bhujal Yojana 2019: groundwater.
Watershed: ridge to valley; community-led.
Irrigation intensity = GIA ÷ NIA × 100.

chapters.title: Seeds, fertilisers, plant protection & farm mechanisation

cards.title: Seed classes
points: Nucleus → breeder (golden yellow tag) → foundation (white tag) → certified (blue tag)
Seed replacement rate: share of area sown with fresh certified/quality seed
Hybrids need fresh seed each season

cards.title: Fertilisers
points: Desired N : P : K ratio ≈ 4 : 2 : 1
Urea: fixed MRP with subsidy; P and K under Nutrient Based Subsidy (2010)
Neem-coated urea (100% from 2015): slows release, curbs diversion
Nano urea (liquid) promoted since 2021

cards.title: Plant protection
cards.body: **Integrated Pest Management (IPM)** combines cultural, mechanical, biological and need-based chemical control to keep pests below the economic threshold. Bio-pesticides and bio-agents (Trichoderma, Trichogramma) are encouraged.

cards.title: Organic and natural farming
cards.body: **PKVY (2015)** promotes cluster-based organic farming; **MOVCDNER** supports organic value chains in the North-East; the **National Mission on Natural Farming** (2024) promotes chemical-free natural farming.

cards.title: Mechanisation
cards.body: The **Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation (SMAM)** supports machinery purchase and **custom hiring centres** so small farmers can rent equipment. Drones are promoted for spraying (e.g. Namo Drone Didi for women SHGs).

cards.q: Certified seed carries a tag of colour:
cards.explain: Breeder: golden yellow; foundation: white; certified: blue.

cards.q: The generally recommended N : P : K ratio is:
cards.explain: Actual use in India has been skewed towards nitrogen.

cards.q: Neem coating of urea mainly:
options: slows nitrogen release and curbs diversion to industry
cards.explain: It improves nitrogen-use efficiency.

notes.p: Good seed, balanced nutrients, water and timely plant protection decide yield. Mechanisation cuts drudgery and costs. For NABARD, connect inputs to credit (KCC), subsidies and sustainability.

The seed chain runs from **nucleus** seed (with the breeder) to **breeder** seed, **foundation** seed and **certified** seed sold to farmers. **Seed replacement rate (SRR)** measures how often farmers use fresh quality seed; higher SRR raises yields, especially for hybrids, which lose vigour if saved seed is reused.

**GM crops:** Bt cotton (2002) is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India; GM mustard (DMH-11) received conditional environmental release in 2022, with the matter before the courts — check the current status.

Macronutrients: N, P, K; secondary: Ca, Mg, S; micronutrients: Zn, B, Fe, etc. Urea contains **46% N**; DAP contains **18% N and 46% P₂O₅**; MOP contains **60% K₂O**.

**Worked example 1:** A crop needs 92 kg N per hectare. Urea needed = 92 ÷ 0.46 = **200 kg**.

**Worked example 2:** If 100 kg DAP is applied, it supplies 18 kg N and 46 kg P₂O₅. To complete 92 kg N, add (92 − 18) ÷ 0.46 ≈ **161 kg urea**.

Imbalanced use (excess urea) harms soil health; the Soil Health Card scheme (2015) recommends nutrients by soil test.

IPM reduces chemical use and costs. Its tools: resistant varieties, crop rotation, trap crops, pheromone traps, bio-control agents and need-based pesticides. **Organic farming** uses no synthetic inputs and requires certification (PGS-India or NPOP). **Natural farming** relies on on-farm inputs such as jeevamrit and mulching.

**Bio-fertilisers** supplement chemical nutrients: **Rhizobium** (legumes), **Azotobacter** and **Azospirillum** (non-legumes, nitrogen fixation), **phosphate-solubilising bacteria**, **mycorrhiza**, and **blue-green algae/Azolla** for paddy. They are cheap and improve soil biology but act slowly.
points: Economic threshold level: pest density at which control is economically justified.

notes.p:
Farm power availability in India has risen but small fragmented holdings limit ownership of machinery. **Custom hiring centres** (often run by FPOs, cooperatives or entrepreneurs) rent tractors, harvesters and seed drills. Equipment such as the **happy seeder** and **super seeder** helps manage paddy stubble without burning. Drones are used for spraying and crop assessment under approved protocols.

**Worked example 3:** A small farmer needs a rotavator for 3 days a year. Buying one costs about ₹1.2 lakh; hiring from a custom hiring centre at ₹1,500 per day costs ₹4,500 a year. Hiring is clearly cheaper — the logic behind custom hiring centres for small holdings.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Foundation seed tag is white; certified is blue.
Urea is 46% N; DAP is 18:46:0.
Only Bt cotton is commercially approved GM crop (check updates).
IPM is not "no pesticides"; it is need-based use.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Seed chain: nucleus → breeder → foundation → certified.
NPK 4:2:1 ideal; NBS 2010.
Neem-coated urea 2015; Soil Health Card 2015.
PKVY 2015; NMNF 2024.
SMAM and custom hiring centres.
Urea 46% N; DAP 18-46-0; MOP 60% K₂O.

chapters.title: Allied sectors: dairy, livestock, fisheries, horticulture & more

cards.title: Dairy
cards.body: India is the **world’s largest milk producer**. **Operation Flood** (launched 1970 by NDDB, founded 1965; Dr Verghese Kurien) built the cooperative **Anand pattern** (village society → district union → state federation).

cards.title: Livestock and poultry
points: 20th Livestock Census (2019): about 536 million livestock (21st census conducted 2024–25; check results)
Rashtriya Gokul Mission (2014): indigenous cattle breeds
National Livestock Mission; Animal Husbandry Infrastructure Development Fund
India is among the top egg and broiler producers

cards.title: Fisheries
points: India: third-largest fish producer, second in aquaculture
PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020): ₹20,050 crore
Fisheries & Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF)
KCC extended to fisheries and animal husbandry (2018–19)

cards.title: Other allied activities
points: Sericulture: India is the second-largest silk producer; all four types — mulberry, tasar, eri, muga (muga unique to Assam)
Apiculture: National Beekeeping & Honey Mission (2020)
Horticulture: MIDH (2014–15); India second in fruits and vegetables

cards.title: Revolutions
cards.body: White — milk; Blue — fisheries; Yellow — oilseeds; Golden — horticulture/honey; Silver — eggs; Green — food grains. Use them for one-liners, not as descriptive answers.

cards.q: Operation Flood was launched in:
cards.explain: NDDB launched it in 1970.

cards.q: Muga silk is produced mainly in:
cards.explain: Golden muga silk is unique to Assam.

cards.q: PM Matsya Sampada Yojana is related to:
cards.explain: Launched in 2020 for the fisheries sector.

notes.p:
Livestock, fisheries and horticulture have grown faster than crop agriculture and provide steadier incomes, especially for small, marginal and landless households and women. NABARD’s refinance and development funds increasingly target these sectors, so they are a favourite in both objective and descriptive questions.

Allied activities also smooth income across the year: milk gives a daily cash flow, while crops pay once or twice a season. This is why banks prefer composite KCC limits and why NABARD promotes integrated farming systems combining crops, livestock, fish and trees on the same farm.

India produces about a quarter of the world’s milk. **Operation Flood** (1970–1996) linked rural producers to urban markets through cooperatives, creating a "flood of milk". The **NDDB** (1965) and **Amul** model (Anand, Gujarat) remain the benchmark.

Schemes: **Rashtriya Gokul Mission** (2014) for indigenous breeds and artificial insemination; **National Programme for Dairy Development**; **Dairy Processing & Infrastructure Development Fund** (with NABARD); **AHIDF** for private investment in processing.

**Worked example 1:** A farmer has 4 cows yielding 10 litres a day for 300 days a year and sells milk at ₹40/litre. Gross income = 4 × 10 × 300 × 40 = **₹4,80,000**. If feed and other costs are 60% of income, net ≈ **₹1,92,000** — showing why dairy loans are attractive when productivity is good.

India is the third-largest fish producer and second in aquaculture; inland fisheries now exceed marine output. **PMMSY** (2020) invests in production, post-harvest infrastructure and fishers’ welfare. Other support: FIDF, **KCC for fishers**, and insurance. Shrimp exports are a major earner.

**Worked example 2:** A one-hectare pond yields 5 tonnes of fish a year sold at ₹120/kg → revenue = 5,000 × 120 = **₹6 lakh**.

India is the second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables. **MIDH** supports nurseries, protected cultivation, post-harvest management and cold chains. **Operation Greens** (2018) targets price stability for tomato, onion and potato (later extended). **Sericulture** — India is the second-largest silk producer and the only country producing all four commercial silks. **Apiculture** — the Sweet Revolution under NBHM.

**Poultry and small ruminants** need little land and give quick returns, making them suitable for landless households and women’s SHGs. Disease control (vaccination, biosecurity against avian influenza) and access to feed and markets decide profitability.
points: Poultry: high growth, integrated contract model in the south.
Goatery and sheep: important for landless and arid regions.

Muga — Assam; tasar — Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh; eri — North-East.
Blue Revolution = fisheries; Silver = eggs.

chapters.title: Agricultural marketing, price policy, credit & insurance

cards.title: Marketing institutions
cards.body: State **APMC** Acts regulate wholesale mandis. **e-NAM** (April 2016) links mandis electronically. A Model APLM Act (2017) encouraged private markets, direct buying and e-trading.

cards.title: Price policy
points: MSP announced for 22 mandated crops; FRP for sugarcane
Recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
Since 2018–19, MSP set at least 1.5 times the A2 + FL cost
Procurement by FCI (1965) and state agencies; PM-AASHA for pulses and oilseeds

cards.title: Agricultural credit

Modified Interest Subvention Scheme: short-term crop loans at 7%; 3% prompt-repayment incentive → effective 4%
Limit under MISS was ₹3 lakh; Budget 2025–26 announced ₹5 lakh — check the operational guidelines
Collateral-free agriculture loans up to ₹2 lakh (raised by RBI from January 2025)

cards.title: Insurance and FPOs
points: PMFBY (2016) and RWBCIS: farmer premium 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial/horticulture
10,000 FPOs scheme (2020)
Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020): ₹1 lakh crore, 3% interest subvention

cards.title: Warehousing
cards.body: The **WDRA** regulates warehouses under the 2007 Act; **electronic negotiable warehouse receipts** let farmers borrow against stored produce instead of selling at harvest-time low prices.

cards.q: e-NAM was launched in:
cards.explain: April 2016.

cards.q: MSP is recommended by:
cards.explain: The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices.

cards.q: With 7% interest and a 3% prompt-repayment incentive, the farmer’s effective rate on a short-term crop loan is:

notes.p:
Farm incomes depend not only on output but also on the price received and the cost of finance and risk. NABARD’s mandate covers rural credit directly, and Phase II descriptive questions frequently ask about MSP, e-NAM, FPOs, KCC and crop insurance.

A useful way to structure answers is the **value chain**: inputs → production → aggregation → storage → processing → marketing, with credit and insurance at each link. Weaknesses at any point — no cold storage, distress sales, delayed payments — reduce the farmer’s share of the consumer rupee.

Most wholesale trade passes through **APMC** mandis; problems include few markets per area, intermediaries’ margins, and delayed payments. Reforms: **e-NAM** (online trading across mandis), private and direct markets under the model act, **FPOs** to aggregate produce, and warehouse-receipt financing.

**MSP** is announced before sowing for 22 crops (14 kharif, 6 rabi, 2 commercial) plus FRP for sugarcane. Since 2018–19, MSP has been fixed at a minimum of 1.5 times the **A2 + FL** cost (paid-out costs plus imputed family labour).

**Worked example 1:** If A2 + FL cost of a crop is ₹1,400 per quintal, MSP should be at least 1.5 × 1,400 = **₹2,100 per quintal**.

The **KCC** scheme (1998) provides revolving credit for crop production, post-harvest needs, consumption and allied activities. Under the **Modified Interest Subvention Scheme**, banks lend short-term crop loans at 7% and prompt repayers receive a further 3% incentive.

**Worked example 2:** A farmer borrows ₹2 lakh for one year under KCC and repays on time. Interest at 7% = ₹14,000; prompt-repayment incentive 3% = ₹6,000. Net cost = **₹8,000 (4%)**.

Credit flow is guided by annual ground-level credit targets and priority-sector norms (18% of ANBC for agriculture, with a sub-target for small and marginal farmers).

**PMFBY** covers yield losses from sowing to post-harvest; **RWBCIS** pays on weather triggers. Farmers pay a small premium; the rest is shared by Centre and states. The **Agriculture Infrastructure Fund** (2020) finances post-harvest infrastructure such as warehouses and cold storage, with interest subvention and credit guarantee. The **10,000 FPOs** scheme provides equity grants and credit guarantees to new FPOs; NABARD, SFAC and NCDC are implementing agencies.
points: FPOs are registered as producer companies or cooperatives.

A2 + FL is not the comprehensive C2 cost.
PSL agriculture target is 18% of ANBC.
MISS effective rate is 4% only on prompt repayment.

MSP: 22 crops + FRP; ≥ 1.5 × A2 + FL.

cards.title: Panchayati Raj
cards.body: The **73rd Amendment (1992)**, in force from 24 April 1993, gave constitutional status to panchayats: three-tier structure, five-year terms, state election and finance commissions, one-third seats for women, and **29 subjects** in the **Eleventh Schedule**.

cards.title: Employment and livelihoods
points: MGNREGA (2005 Act): 100 days of wage work per rural household per year
DAY-NRLM (2011): SHG-based livelihoods; "Lakhpati Didi" initiative
DDU-GKY (2014): placement-linked skilling for rural youth
PMEGP: subsidy-linked self-employment

cards.title: Infrastructure programmes
points: PMGSY (2000): all-weather rural roads
PMAY-Gramin (2016): pucca houses
Jal Jeevan Mission (2019): tap water to every rural household
SBM-Gramin: sanitation; SVAMITVA (2020): drone-based property cards

cards.title: NABARD’s role
cards.body: **SHG–Bank Linkage Programme** (pilot 1992), **RIDF** (1995–96) for state rural infrastructure, watershed and tribal development funds, and promotion of FPOs and JLGs.

cards.title: Answer frame
cards.body: Rural development answers: define (economic + social + institutional) → key programmes → convergence through PRIs and SHGs → gaps (leakages, capacity, convergence) → role of NABARD and banks.

cards.q: The Eleventh Schedule lists how many subjects for panchayats?
cards.explain: 29 subjects; the Twelfth Schedule has 18 for municipalities.

cards.q: PMGSY, the rural roads programme, was launched in:
cards.explain: December 2000.

cards.q: NABARD launched the SHG–Bank Linkage pilot in:
cards.explain: 1992 pilot of linking 500 SHGs with banks.

notes.p:
Rural development means improving the economic and social well-being of rural people: incomes and jobs, infrastructure (roads, water, power, housing), human development (health, education) and empowerment (local governance, women’s groups). About 65% of India’s population lives in rural areas (Census 2011: 68.8%), so the theme runs through ESI and ARD alike.

Approaches have evolved from the **Community Development Programme** (1952) and the Integrated Rural Development Programme (1978–80) to rights-based laws (MGNREGA, NFSA, RTE) and the current focus on saturation of basic services through convergence and digital delivery (DBT).

**Panchayati Raj Institutions** (gram panchayat, panchayat samiti, zila parishad) plan and implement local development; the **Gram Sabha** is the village assembly of voters. **SHGs** and their federations under DAY-NRLM are the backbone of livelihood programmes. **Cooperatives**, **FPOs** and **RRBs** deliver credit and services.

The Ministry of Cooperation (2021) is computerising PACS and promoting multipurpose PACS.

**Worked recall example:** "Which institution at the village level approves MGNREGA works and conducts social audits?" → the **Gram Sabha**. Social audits improve transparency and reduce leakages.

**MGNREGA** guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment to every rural household that demands it, with wages paid by DBT and works such as water conservation and rural connectivity. **DAY-NRLM** mobilises poor women into SHGs, provides revolving funds and bank linkage, and aims to create "Lakhpati Didis" (annual household income of at least ₹1 lakh).

**Worked example 1:** A household works 100 days under MGNREGA at a notified wage of ₹300/day (wages differ by state; this is an illustration). Earnings = 100 × 300 = **₹30,000** in the year.

**Worked example 2:** An SHG of 10 members saves ₹200 each per month for 12 months = ₹24,000. With bank linkage at a 1:4 savings-to-credit ratio, it could access about **₹96,000** — showing how savings leverage credit.

**PMGSY** (2000) connects eligible habitations with all-weather roads. **PMAY-G** (2016) builds pucca houses with basic amenities. **Jal Jeevan Mission** (2019) provides functional household tap connections. **SBM-G** made villages open-defecation free and now focuses on solid and liquid waste management. **SVAMITVA** (2020) maps rural residential land with drones and issues property cards, enabling loans against property. **RIDF** (NABARD, 1995–96) funds state rural infrastructure using banks’ PSL shortfall deposits.

Convergence — combining MGNREGA labour with other scheme funds for the same asset — is a recurring answer point.
points: National Panchayati Raj Day: 24 April.
Rural share of population (Census 2011): 68.8%.

MGNREGA is demand-driven, not target-based.
RIDF is funded from PSL shortfall deposits.

cards.title: Food security
cards.body: Availability, access, utilisation and stability. The **National Food Security Act, 2013** covers up to **75% of rural and 50% of urban** population: **5 kg** of grain per person per month for priority households and **35 kg** per household for Antyodaya families.

cards.title: Free grain
cards.body: Under **PMGKAY**, grains under NFSA are distributed free; in 2023 the government extended free grain for five years from 1 January 2024.

cards.title: Climate and agriculture
points: NAPCC (2008): 8 missions incl. National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture
NICRA (ICAR, 2011): climate-resilient agriculture research
Climate risks: heat stress on wheat, erratic monsoon, floods, pests
Adaptation: drought-tolerant varieties, micro-irrigation, crop diversification, insurance

cards.title: Forestry
points: National Forest Policy 1988: target one-third of area under forest/tree cover
India State of Forest Report (FSI): biennial
National Agroforestry Policy (2014) — India was among the first countries to adopt one
Joint Forest Management: communities share in protection and benefits

cards.title: Answer frame
cards.body: Link food security to production (productivity, irrigation), access (PDS, ONORC, incomes), nutrition (fortified rice, millets) and stability (buffer stocks, climate resilience).

cards.q: Under NFSA, priority households receive per person per month:
cards.explain: Antyodaya households get 35 kg per household.

cards.q: The National Forest Policy 1988 targets forest/tree cover over:
cards.explain: One-third of geographical area.

cards.q: NICRA, a project on climate-resilient agriculture, is run by:
cards.explain: National Innovations in Climate Resilient Agriculture (2011).

notes.p:
India moved from food shortages in the 1960s to surplus grain production after the **Green Revolution** (HYV seeds, irrigation, fertilisers in Punjab, Haryana and western UP). Today the challenges are **nutrition** (stunting, anaemia), **sustainability** (groundwater, soil health) and **climate risk**.

The **NFSA, 2013** made food a legal entitlement, delivered through the **Targeted PDS**. **One Nation One Ration Card** allows portability across states. **Fortified rice** is distributed through government schemes to tackle micronutrient deficiencies. Millets ("Shree Anna") are promoted for nutrition and climate resilience; 2023 was the International Year of Millets at India’s initiative.

The **FCI** procures wheat and rice at MSP and maintains **buffer stocks** against quarterly norms; excess stocks are offloaded through the Open Market Sale Scheme to cool prices.

**Worked example 1:** A state has 2 crore NFSA beneficiaries (priority households). Monthly requirement = 2 crore × 5 kg = 10 crore kg = **1 lakh tonnes**; yearly ≈ **12 lakh tonnes**.

**Worked example 2:** If PDS leakage falls from 20% to 10% on 12 lakh tonnes allocated, an extra **1.2 lakh tonnes** reaches beneficiaries — why Aadhaar-seeded ePoS machines matter.

**Decentralised procurement (DCP):** states procure and distribute grain themselves, with the Centre reimbursing costs, which cuts transport and storage expenses. The **Price Stabilisation Fund** supports buffers of pulses and onions to manage consumer price spikes.

Rising temperatures shorten crop durations and cut yields (terminal heat stress in wheat), monsoon variability increases droughts and floods, and pests spread to new areas. **Adaptation**: climate-resilient varieties, conservation agriculture, micro-irrigation, crop diversification, weather-based advisories, insurance. **Mitigation**: lower methane from paddy (alternate wetting and drying, direct-seeded rice), better livestock feed, agroforestry and reduced stubble burning.

NABARD is an accredited entity for international climate funds (Adaptation Fund, Green Climate Fund) — a frequent interview point.

**Forest Survey of India** publishes the biennial **India State of Forest Report**; check the latest edition for figures. Policies: **National Forest Policy 1988** (33% target), **Forest Rights Act 2006** (rights of forest-dwelling communities), **Green India Mission** (under NAPCC), **CAMPA** funds for compensatory afforestation. **Agroforestry** — trees on farms — diversifies income and stores carbon.

**Worked recall example:** "Which Act recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers over forest land and produce?" → the **Forest Rights Act, 2006**. Under it, the Gram Sabha initiates the process of determining claims.
points: Land degradation and desertification affect a large share of India’s land; India aims to restore 26 million ha of degraded land by 2030.

5 kg per person; 35 kg per AAY household.
Forest policy target: one-third of area.
NICRA is ICAR’s, not NABARD’s.

notes.p: Key points.

ONORC; fortified rice; millets 2023.
NAPCC 2008: 8 missions; NMSA.
NICRA 2011 (ICAR).

cards.title: NABARD
cards.body: Established on **12 July 1982** under the NABARD Act, 1981, on the recommendation of the **CRAFICARD** committee (B. Sivaraman). It took over the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation and RBI’s rural credit functions. It is now wholly owned by the Government of India.

cards.title: Functions
points: Refinance to cooperatives, RRBs and commercial banks
Direct lending: RIDF, LTIF, infrastructure for states
Supervision: statutory inspection of RRBs and state/district cooperative banks
Development: SHG–BLP, JLGs, FPOs, watershed, tribal development, financial inclusion

cards.title: Rural credit structure
points: Short-term cooperatives: StCB → DCCB → PACS
Long-term cooperatives: SCARDB → PCARDB
RRBs (RRB Act 1976): Centre 50%, sponsor bank 35%, state 15%
Commercial banks, SFBs, MFIs, NBFC-MFIs

cards.title: RRB consolidation
cards.body: RRBs were amalgamated in phases following a "**One State, One RRB**" approach; the 2025 round reduced their number to 28 (check the latest list). The first RRB, Prathama Bank, opened on 2 October 1975.

cards.title: Subsidiaries
cards.body: NABCONS (consultancy), NABKISAN (FPO finance), NABSAMRUDDHI (non-farm finance), NABFINS (microfinance), NABVENTURES (venture capital), NABFOUNDATION, NABSANRAKSHAN (credit guarantees).

cards.q: NABARD was set up on the recommendation of:
cards.explain: Committee to Review Arrangements for Institutional Credit for Agriculture and Rural Development.

cards.q: Shareholding of the Central Government, sponsor bank and state government in an RRB is:
cards.explain: Centre 50%, sponsor 35%, state 15%.

cards.q: PACS operate at the level of:
cards.explain: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies are the base tier.

notes.p:
NABARD is the apex development finance institution for agriculture and rural development. Its three roles are **financial** (refinance and direct finance), **supervisory** (cooperative banks and RRBs) and **developmental** (institution building, innovation, capacity building). Its head office is in **Mumbai**. The NABARD Act was amended in 2017–18 to raise authorised capital and transfer RBI’s remaining stake to the Government.

NABARD also prepares **Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs)** for every district, estimating credit potential sector-wise; these feed into the district credit plans of lead banks under the **Lead Bank Scheme** (1969).

**RIDF** (1995–96): loans to states for rural infrastructure — irrigation, roads, bridges, social sector — funded by banks’ PSL shortfall deposits. **LTIF** (2016–17) for irrigation projects; **Micro Irrigation Fund**, **Dairy Processing & Infrastructure Development Fund**, **Fisheries & Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund**, **Warehouse Infrastructure Fund**, **Food Processing Fund**; plus the **Watershed Development Fund**, **Tribal Development Fund** and **Financial Inclusion Fund**.

**Worked example 1:** A bank’s agriculture PSL shortfall is ₹500 crore. It may be required to deposit this amount in RIDF (or a similar fund) at a below-market rate. The money then finances state rural infrastructure — so a bank’s shortfall still reaches rural areas.

**Short-term structure** (crop loans): State Cooperative Bank → District Central Cooperative Bank → **PACS** at the village level. **Long-term structure** (investment credit): SCARDB → PCARDB. Weaknesses: governance, dual control, low capital, high NPAs; reforms include **computerisation of PACS**, model bye-laws allowing multipurpose PACS, and RBI supervision of cooperative banks under the amended Banking Regulation Act (2020).

**Worked example 2 (SHG–BLP):** NABARD’s SHG–Bank Linkage has grown into one of the world’s largest microfinance programmes. If an SHG with ₹50,000 in savings receives credit of four times its corpus, it can borrow **₹2 lakh** — the leverage ratio banks commonly use for repeat linkages.

RRBs were set up under the **RRB Act, 1976** to combine cooperative local touch with commercial bank professionalism. Ownership: **Centre 50%, sponsor bank 35%, state 15%**. They must lend 75% of ANBC to the priority sector. Successive amalgamations (from 196 RRBs to far fewer) aimed at scale and technology; the 2025 round followed the "one state, one RRB" principle and brought the total to 28 — verify against the latest RBI/DFS list.

cards.title: Growth vs development
cards.body: **Economic growth** is a rise in real output (GDP). **Development** is broader: better health, education, living standards, equity and freedom. Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.

cards.title: National income aggregates
points: GDP at market prices − depreciation = NDP
GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA) = GNP
NNP at factor cost = NNP at MP − net indirect taxes = national income
GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies = GDP
Per capita income = national income ÷ population

cards.title: Measuring development
cards.body: **Human Development Index** (UNDP): health (life expectancy), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP), combined by a **geometric mean**. Also: MPI, Gender Development Index, Gender Inequality Index.

cards.title: Sustainable development
cards.body: "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" — **Brundtland Report (1987)**. The UN’s **2030 Agenda** has **17 SDGs** and 169 targets; NITI Aayog publishes the SDG India Index.

cards.title: Real vs nominal
cards.body: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses base-year prices. Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation (GDP deflator). MoSPI periodically revises the base year — check the current series.

cards.q: Which three dimensions make up the HDI?
cards.explain: Long and healthy life, knowledge, decent standard of living.

cards.q: NNP at factor cost is also called:
cards.explain: National income = NNP at factor cost.

cards.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there?
cards.explain: 17 SDGs under the 2030 Agenda (2015).

notes.p: "Growth and Development" is the first block of the ESI syllabus for RBI Grade B and appears in NABARD ESI too. Objective questions test definitions and indices; descriptive questions ask you to distinguish growth from development, evaluate inclusive growth, or discuss sustainability.

Three methods give the same total in principle: **production (value added)**, **income** (wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income) and **expenditure** (C + I + G + X − M).

**Worked example 1:** GDP at market prices = ₹200 lakh crore; depreciation = ₹20; NFIA = −₹5; net indirect taxes = ₹15 (all in lakh crore).
GNP at MP = 200 − 5 = **195**.
NNP at MP = 195 − 20 = **175**.
NNP at FC (national income) = 175 − 15 = **160**.
If population is 140 crore, per capita national income = 160 lakh crore ÷ 140 crore ≈ **₹1.14 lakh**.

India reports **GVA at basic prices** by sector and GDP at market prices; growth is usually quoted in real terms.

**Worked example 2:** Nominal GDP rises from ₹300 lakh crore to ₹330 lakh crore (10%), while the GDP deflator rises 4%. Real growth ≈ 10 − 4 = **6%** (exactly 1.10/1.04 − 1 ≈ 5.8%).

GDP has limits as a welfare measure: it ignores distribution, unpaid household work, environmental damage and leisure. Hence alternative measures — HDI, green GDP, happiness indices.

**HDI** (UNDP, since 1990) combines life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and GNI per capita (PPP) through a geometric mean, so poor performance in one dimension cannot be fully offset by another. **MPI** (UNDP–OPHI) counts deprivations in health, education and living standards; NITI Aayog publishes a **national MPI** using NFHS data. **Gender Inequality Index** covers reproductive health, empowerment and labour market participation.

For the latest ranks and values, refer to the most recent Human Development Report — they change annually.

**Inclusive growth** means growth whose benefits reach all sections — through jobs, access to finance, education and health. **Sustainable development** balances economic, social and environmental goals across generations. In descriptive answers, link: financial inclusion (PMJDY), skill development, social protection and green finance as instruments of inclusive and sustainable growth.
points: Kuznets curve: inequality first rises then falls with income (a hypothesis, debated).
Environmental Kuznets curve: pollution first rises then falls with income.

notes.p: Define terms in the first two lines, add one data point or example, give two to three arguments, and close with a balanced conclusion. Avoid quoting numbers you are unsure of; use qualitative phrasing ("India has seen a steady rise in HDI value over three decades").
Key points.
points: Growth = output; development = well-being.
GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − depreciation.
National income = NNP at factor cost.
HDI: health, education, income; geometric mean.
Brundtland 1987; 17 SDGs (2030 Agenda).
Real growth ≈ nominal − inflation.

cards.title: Poverty lines in India
cards.body: Expert groups: **Lakdawala (1993)**, **Tendulkar (2009)** — 21.9% poverty in 2011–12, **Rangarajan (2014)** — 29.5% for 2011–12. NITI Aayog’s **national MPI** measures multidimensional deprivation using NFHS data.

cards.title: Labour market measures
points: Labour force = employed + unemployed (seeking/available)
LFPR = labour force ÷ population × 100
WPR = employed ÷ population × 100
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
PLFS (NSO) gives usual status and current weekly status estimates

cards.title: Types of unemployment
cards.body: **Structural** (skill or sector mismatch), **frictional** (between jobs), **cyclical** (demand slump), **seasonal** (agriculture), **disguised** (more workers than needed; marginal product ≈ 0), **educated** unemployment.

cards.title: Inequality
cards.body: The **Lorenz curve** plots cumulative income share against population share; the **Gini coefficient** = area between the equality line and the Lorenz curve ÷ total area under the equality line (0 = perfect equality, 1 = extreme inequality).

cards.title: Descriptive frame
cards.body: For poverty or jobs answers: causes → current status (cite PLFS/MPI qualitatively) → government measures → gaps → way forward. It fits most questions.

cards.q: Disguised unemployment means:
options: workers whose marginal productivity is near zero
cards.explain: Removing them does not reduce output.

cards.q: Of 1,000 persons aged 15+, 560 are employed and 40 unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
The poverty line estimate of 21.9% for 2011–12 is based on the methodology of the:
cards.explain: Rangarajan gave 29.5% for the same year.

notes.p: **Absolute poverty** is the inability to meet a minimum standard of consumption; **relative poverty** compares with others in society. India historically measured absolute poverty with **consumption-based poverty lines** set by expert groups. The **Tendulkar** methodology moved away from calorie norms to a basket of goods and services; the **Rangarajan** group (2014) raised the line. No official poverty line has been notified after these; the government and researchers now often refer to **multidimensional poverty** and to household consumption surveys (HCES 2022–23 and 2023–24).

NITI Aayog’s **National MPI** uses 12 indicators across health (nutrition, child and adolescent mortality, maternal health), education (years of schooling, attendance) and standard of living (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account). A household is MPI-poor if it is deprived in at least one-third of weighted indicators. NITI reports have shown a large fall in multidimensional poverty over the last decade — quote the current report’s figure only if you are sure of it.

The **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)** by the NSO provides annual estimates on **usual status** (reference year) and **current weekly status** (reference week), plus quarterly urban and, since 2025, monthly bulletins.

**Worked example 1:** Population aged 15+ = 1,000; employed = 560; unemployed = 40.
Labour force = 600 → **LFPR = 60%**.
**WPR = 56%**.
**Unemployment rate = 40/600 = 6.67%**.

**Worked example 2:** If 50 discouraged persons start seeking work and none find it, labour force = 650, unemployed = 90 → UR = 90/650 ≈ **13.8%**, even though employment did not fall. This is why unemployment rates can rise when job-seeking increases.

Inequality is measured by the **Gini coefficient**, income/consumption shares of top and bottom deciles, and the **Palma ratio** (top 10% ÷ bottom 40%). Consumption-based Gini is usually lower than income- or wealth-based Gini. Policy levers: progressive taxation, public spending on health and education, transfers, minimum wages and financial inclusion.

**Worked example 3:** If the top 10% of households account for 30% of consumption and the bottom 40% for 20%, the **Palma ratio** = 30 ÷ 20 = **1.5**. A rising Palma ratio signals that gains are concentrating at the top even if average consumption grows.

Wage employment: **MGNREGA** (100 days guaranteed). Self-employment and livelihoods: **DAY-NRLM** (SHGs), **PMEGP**, **MUDRA**. Skilling: **PMKVY**, **DDU-GKY**. Social protection: NFSA (subsidised grain), PM-JAY, pensions. Urban: **DAY-NULM**, PM SVANidhi. Labour reforms: four labour codes consolidating 29 central laws.

Link skill gaps to structural unemployment.

cards.title: 1991 crisis and reforms
cards.body: A balance-of-payments crisis in 1991 (reserves covering only weeks of imports) led to **LPG reforms**: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation — delicensing, opening to FDI, trade and tariff cuts, financial-sector reforms, and rupee devaluation.

cards.title: Industrial policy milestones
points: IPR 1948: mixed economy
IPR 1956: public sector leads (Schedules A, B, C)
NIP 1991: end of licence raj for most industries; MRTP curbs removed; PSU reform
2014: Make in India; 2020: PLI schemes; Atmanirbhar Bharat

cards.title: Privatisation and disinvestment
cards.body: **Disinvestment** sells part of government equity; **strategic sale** transfers management control (e.g. Air India to the Tata group, 2022). **New PSE Policy (2021)** keeps a minimal presence in strategic sectors; DIPAM manages the process.

cards.title: Labour codes
cards.body: 29 central labour laws were merged into four codes: **Code on Wages (2019)**, **Industrial Relations Code (2020)**, **Code on Social Security (2020)** and **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020)**. Check the current status of central and state rules.

cards.title: Answer frame
cards.body: For reform questions: background → key measures → outcomes (growth, FDI, competition) → criticisms (jobless growth, agrarian distress, inequality) → way forward.

cards.q: The immediate trigger for India’s 1991 reforms was:
cards.explain: Forex reserves fell to very low levels.

cards.q: How many labour codes replaced the earlier central labour laws?
cards.explain: Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH.

cards.q: Which policy first divided industries into three schedules with a leading role for the public sector?
cards.explain: Schedule A was reserved for the State.

notes.p:
After independence, India followed a **mixed economy** with the public sector at the "commanding heights" (IPR 1948, IPR 1956) and an extensive **licensing** system. The **Planning Commission** (1950) ran Five-Year Plans until it was replaced by **NITI Aayog** in 2015, which works as a policy think tank promoting cooperative federalism.

By the late 1980s, fiscal deficits, rising external debt and the Gulf war oil shock produced the **1991 BoP crisis**.

Main measures:
- **Industrial**: abolition of licensing except for a short list; MRTP asset limits removed; public-sector reservation cut.
- **Trade**: tariff cuts, removal of quantitative restrictions, current-account convertibility (1994).
- **Foreign investment**: automatic approval for FDI in many sectors; FPI allowed.
- **Financial**: Narasimham Committee reforms — lower CRR/SLR, interest-rate deregulation, entry of private banks, prudential norms.
- **Fiscal**: tax reform and deficit reduction.

Outcomes: faster growth, rising FDI, services-led expansion. Criticisms: limited manufacturing jobs, agrarian distress, regional and income inequality.

In descriptive answers, note the sequencing: **stabilisation** (fiscal correction, devaluation, IMF support) came first, followed by **structural reforms** (industrial, trade, financial). Second-generation reforms later covered insurance, pensions, GST, the IBC and labour law.

**Make in India** (2014) aims to raise manufacturing; **Production Linked Incentive (PLI)** schemes (from 2020) reward incremental sales in sectors such as mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and solar modules. **MSMEs** are classified by investment and turnover; the limits were raised from April 2025 (micro up to ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover; small up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore; medium up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore) — verify against the latest notification.

**Worked example 1:** A firm with ₹4 crore investment in plant and machinery and ₹30 crore turnover is classified as **small** under the revised limits, because it exceeds the micro investment cap of ₹2.5 crore.

The **four labour codes** aim to simplify compliance, widen social security (including gig and platform workers under the Social Security Code), define a national floor wage, and ease rules on standing orders and retrenchment for larger firms. Debates: flexibility vs job security, implementation through state rules, and coverage of informal workers. Around 90% of India’s workforce is informal, so social security portability (e-Shram portal, launched 2021) is a key theme.

**Worked example 2:** Under the IR Code, the threshold for prior government permission for lay-off/retrenchment/closure rose from 100 to **300 workers**, with states allowed to vary it. In a descriptive answer, present both sides: flexibility for firms vs worker protection.
Mix-ups to avoid.

chapters.title: Balance of payments, exchange rates & globalisation

cards.title: BoP structure
points: Current account: merchandise trade + invisibles (services, primary income, transfers/remittances)
Capital account: FDI, FPI, external commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, banking capital
Overall balance ⇒ change in forex reserves
CAD = imports of goods & services + net outflows − exports − inflows on current items

cards.title: Exchange rate regimes
cards.body: India follows a **market-determined (managed float)** rate since 1993, with RBI intervention to curb volatility. **NEER** is a weighted average against trading partners; **REER** adjusts NEER for relative inflation.

cards.title: Depreciation effects
cards.body: A weaker rupee makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. It may widen the trade gap in the short run (J-curve) before improving it, and it adds to imported inflation (especially oil).

cards.title: Globalisation and WTO
cards.body: **WTO** (1995) agreements: goods (GATT), services (GATS), intellectual property (TRIPS), Agreement on Agriculture — subsidy boxes: **amber** (trade-distorting), **blue** (production-limiting), **green** (minimally distorting).

cards.title: Answer frame
cards.body: For CAD questions: define → components → causes (oil, gold, services surplus, remittances) → financing (FDI vs volatile FPI) → policy measures.

cards.q: Remittances from Indians abroad are recorded in the:
cards.explain: They are current transfers (secondary income).

cards.q: REER differs from NEER because it adjusts for:
cards.explain: REER = NEER adjusted for price differences.

cards.q: Under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture, minimally trade-distorting subsidies fall in the:
cards.explain: Green box subsidies are not capped.

notes.p: The external sector links India to world demand, capital flows and commodity prices. RBI Grade B questions ask about BoP trends, rupee movements, FDI policy, forex reserves and trade agreements. Use RBI’s quarterly BoP releases for current figures.

The BoP records all transactions between residents and non-residents.

**Current account:** goods trade (India usually runs a large deficit), services (a large surplus led by software and business services), primary income (investment income, usually a deficit), and secondary income (remittances — India is the world’s largest recipient).
**Capital/financial account:** FDI, FPI, ECBs, NRI deposits, trade credit.

**Worked example 1 (US$ billion):** goods exports 450, goods imports 700, net services +160, net primary income −40, net transfers +110.
Current account = 450 − 700 + 160 − 40 + 110 = **−20** (a CAD of $20 billion).
If net capital inflows are $45 billion, the overall balance is **+25**, added to reserves.

Under a floating regime, demand for and supply of dollars set the rupee’s value. The RBI intervenes in spot and forward markets to smooth volatility, not to defend a fixed level.

**Worked example 2:** The rupee moves from ₹80 to ₹84 per dollar. Rupee depreciation = (84 − 80)/80 = **5%** in rupee terms; the dollar appreciated 5%. An exporter earning $1 million now receives ₹84 million instead of ₹80 million.

**Convertibility:** full on current account since 1994; partial on capital account, liberalised over time under FEMA, 1999.

**Forex reserves** comprise foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF. Adequacy is judged by **import cover** (months of imports reserves can pay for) and by the ratio of reserves to short-term external debt. The RBI publishes reserves weekly in its Weekly Statistical Supplement.

FDI enters through the **automatic route** (no prior approval) or the **government route**. Sectoral caps apply (e.g. insurance raised to 100% in Budget 2025–26 for companies investing the entire premium in India — check notification). FDI is stable and brings technology; FPI is volatile ("hot money").

**Globalisation** — integration through trade, capital, technology and people — raised growth and service exports but exposed India to global shocks and import competition. India has signed recent trade agreements (e.g. with the UAE and Australia in 2022, EFTA in 2024, and the UK in 2025); verify current status before writing.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Remittances are current account, not capital account.
A CAD is financed by capital inflows or reserves.
Depreciation helps exporters but raises import costs.
Green box (allowed) vs amber box (capped).

notes.p: Key points.
points: BoP = current + capital/financial account.
India: goods deficit, services surplus, high remittances.

NEER vs REER (inflation-adjusted).

chapters.title: Demography, social sector & the Indian political system

cards.title: Census 2011 facts
points: Population: about 121 crore
Sex ratio: 943 females per 1,000 males
Literacy: 74.04%
Urban share: 31.1%
Next Census: scheduled for 2027 (reference date 1 March 2027 for most areas; check notification)

cards.title: Demographic dividend
cards.body: A rising share of working-age population (15–64) can boost growth if people are healthy, skilled and employed. India’s window is expected to last into the 2040s; the payoff depends on jobs and human capital.

cards.title: Education and health
cards.body: **RTE Act, 2009** (free and compulsory education for ages 6–14, Art. 21A). **NEP 2020**: 5+3+3+4 structure, mother-tongue instruction in early years, multidisciplinary higher education. Health: **NHM**, **Ayushman Bharat** (health and wellness centres + PM-JAY).

cards.title: Political system essentials
cards.body: Parliamentary democracy; federal structure with a strong Centre; **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** created constitutional status for panchayats and municipalities; Directive Principles guide social policy.

cards.title: Social justice
cards.body: "Positive discrimination" means reservations and targeted schemes for SCs, STs, OBCs and EWS; in answers, discuss both outcomes and implementation gaps.

cards.q: Sex ratio in Census 2011 was:
cards.explain: 943 females per 1,000 males.

cards.q: Which constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions?
cards.explain: 73rd Amendment (1992); 74th for urban local bodies.

cards.q: The 5+3+3+4 school structure was introduced by:
cards.explain: It replaces the 10+2 structure.

notes.p:
The **demographic transition** has four stages: high birth and death rates → falling death rates (population boom) → falling birth rates → low birth and death rates. India is in the late third stage: the total fertility rate fell to about the replacement level of 2.1 (NFHS-5, 2019–21: 2.0), though it varies widely across states.

**Worked example 1 (dependency ratio):** Population aged 0–14 = 350 million, 65+ = 100 million, 15–64 = 950 million.
Dependency ratio = (350 + 100) ÷ 950 × 100 ≈ **47.4**. A falling ratio means more workers per dependant — the basis of the demographic dividend.

Urban share rose to **31.1%** in Census 2011 and is estimated to be higher today. Issues: housing, informal settlements, transport, water and waste. Programmes: **Smart Cities Mission**, **AMRUT**, **PMAY-U**, **Swachh Bharat (Urban)**. Migration is largely internal and short-distance; seasonal migrants face gaps in social security, addressed partly by **One Nation One Ration Card** and the e-Shram portal.

**Worked example 2 (urban growth):** If a town grows from 2,00,000 to 2,42,000 people over two years, the compound annual growth rate is √(2,42,000 ÷ 2,00,000) − 1 = √1.21 − 1 = **10%** a year — a pace that would double the population in about seven years, straining services planned for the original size.

**Education:** near-universal enrolment at the primary level; challenges are learning outcomes, dropouts at secondary level and teacher quality. **NEP 2020** aims at foundational literacy and numeracy (NIPUN Bharat), flexible higher education, and a target of 50% gross enrolment ratio in higher education by 2035.

**Health:** public spending on health has historically been low as a share of GDP; out-of-pocket expenditure is high but has been falling. Ayushman Bharat combines primary care through **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** and hospital insurance through **PM-JAY**.

Constitutional provisions: Articles 15(4), 16(4) (reservations), 17 (abolition of untouchability), 46 (promotion of weaker sections). EWS reservation of 10% (103rd Amendment, 2019) was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022. Gender issues: low female LFPR (rising in recent PLFS rounds), sex ratio at birth, safety and political representation — the **Women’s Reservation Act, 2023** (106th Amendment) reserves one-third of seats in Lok Sabha and state assemblies, effective after the next delimitation.

India is a **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic** with a parliamentary system: the President is the constitutional head, the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. **Federalism** distributes powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule). Local self-government: the 73rd (Panchayats, Part IX) and 74th (Municipalities, Part IXA) Amendments. Cooperative federalism is institutionalised through NITI Aayog and the GST Council.
